issues.issue: The State's promise to file an amended count says only that the Defendant "does not object," which is neither a plea nor an admission, and the provision never says what becomes of the original count or of Count II on successful completion. Whether non-objection carries any concession of guilt is left open on the face of the words.

"[I]t is the responsibility of the Defendant to show the Prosecutor's Office that he has completed all the terms" fixes no form, standard or deadline for that showing. The clause is also a fragment severed from the suspension-of-prosecution sentence that would give it a time frame.

"[I]f he fails to comply" is unqualified by materiality, cure or any mechanism for determining non-compliance, so any lapse however trivial appears to trigger redocketing. Nothing in the provision says who decides, or on what proof, that a failure has occurred.

The waiver of speedy trial and of Criminal Rule 4 time limits is stated without any temporal boundary, and the truncated lead-in ("Program.") leaves unclear whether the waiver runs only during the diversion period or survives it. The provision therefore does not say what period of delay the Defendant has agreed to absorb.

The jury-trial waiver breaks off mid-sentence — "On the charge(s) Jn this." — so the charges to which the waiver attaches are not identified in the words themselves. Whether it reaches only the original count or also the amended Count II added under paragraph I cannot be read off the text.

This provision makes trial by judge operative only "in the event that the Defendant fails to comply ... and prosecution is resumed," while the immediately preceding jury waiver (c005) is stated unconditionally. The two cannot both be read literally as to when, and on which charges, the jury right is given up.

This stipulation admits knowing, injurious touching of Beth Marriott but produces no conviction, while section 14.1.A of Haywood's University of Pittsburgh employment contract defines just cause as "conduct by Employee resulting in his conviction of a violation of a criminal statute." Whether an admission made in a diversion agreement satisfies that clause, or must instead be routed through 14.1.F's "conduct ... seriously prejudicial to the best interests of the University," is precisely what has to be construed.

The "Specifically, the Defendant admits" sentence ends mid-clause — "got into an argument and" — so the specific conduct admitted is missing from the instrument. What the Defendant conceded beyond the general stipulation cannot be determined from the words.

The provision directs payment "as instructed at the time of signing this agreement" and then sets payment "in full due by March 11, 2011," two different times for the same obligation. Whether the fees were due at signing or by the later date is not resolved within the clause.

The condition runs "during the 'ten of this agreement" — a mechanical error for "term" — and no term of the agreement is anywhere defined, only a dismissal date in the closing paragraph. The period during which the no-offense condition binds therefore has to be supplied by construction.
"[A]n approved agency" is not defined and the provision does not say who approves or by what criteria. Nor does it fix what an "evaluation for treatment and/or counseling" must consist of.

"[P]articipate in any counseling recommended" is open-ended as to who may recommend it, how much of it, and for how long, with no cap tied to any date in the agreement. The obligation as written could outrun the diversion period itself.

"Proof of evaluation must be made by March 11, 2011" does not say in what form proof is made or to whom it must be delivered. It also leaves unstated whether the underlying evaluation, as opposed to the proof, must be completed by that date.

The promise that evaluation and counseling information "would not otherwise be available to the public or for publication" names no custodian, no exceptions and no consequence for disclosure. Whether it bars release to non-public third parties, such as the Defendant's employer, is not addressed by the words used.
"60 hours of Community Service" is not defined and the provision names no agency to perform it with, to approve it, or to verify the hours. Only the deadline is fixed.

"[A]t reasonable times" and "all reasonable inquires" set no measurable boundary on the reporting and interrogation obligation, which extends to "all Law Enforcement Agencies" without limit as to subject. The catch-all is then followed by "including information concerning the allegations in this case," leaving unclear whether the duty is confined to this case or general.

The promise that "[t]his information will not be used against Defendant" upon redocketing cannot be squared with the section IV stipulations (c009), which are express admissions of the offense conduct given in the same agreement and plainly intended to be available if prosecution resumes. Which body of information the shield covers — only answers given under paragraph E, or the stipulations too — is the thing to construe.

"[A]ny changes in address, phone number, and/or employment" is undefined as to what counts as a change in employment (loss of a job, a new position, a change of duties). The seven-day clock therefore has no identifiable starting event in some cases.

The February 10, 2012 dismissal date stands against performance deadlines that all fall much earlier — fees by March 11, 2011 (c011) and community service by August 3, 2011 (c017) — and against the undefined "term" in the no-offense condition (c012). Whether the Defendant remains bound, and subject to redocketing, between the last deadline and the dismissal date is not resolved when the instrument is read as a whole.

This closing acknowledgment says non-compliance means the agreement "will automatically be revoked" and a summons issued, while paragraph II (c003) says the case "will be redocketed for court and prosecution resumed" and c002 makes the Defendant responsible for showing completion. The two describe different consequences and different mechanics, and neither provides for any determination before revocation.
